description: We are a team of creative and passionate individuals interested in technology, problem solving, and innovation. We aim to bring together people with different skills and perspectives to develop creative solutions to real world challenges related to Earth and space.
summary:
Vyoma is a browser based Mars outpost game that trains 10–15 year olds to think like mission planners. Players land in one of six sectors based on real Mars regions, such as Gale Crater and Hellas Planitia, then build and run a base that must keep a crew of four alive for 30 sols. Every building makes or uses power, oxygen, water or food, so every choice is a real engineering trade off : cheap solar power or a storm proof reactor, radiation shielding or crop growth. Dust storms, solar particle events and equipment failures force decisions, each paired with the true mission story behind it. The mission can genuinely fail, and when it does, a debrief explains why in plain language, along with the real science.
Vyoma answers the challenge by training decision making, not memorization. Its life-support and radiation numbers come from NASA sources, including the Life Support Baseline Values document and Curiosity's radiation measurements. It matters because future crews will live or die by these trade offs, and Vyoma lets young learners practice them safely.
details:
Vyoma: a Mars outpost trainer for junior astronauts

What it is: a web game (runs in any browser, nothing to install) for learners aged 10 to 15. Play: https://amaleshwaren.github.io/vyoma/

How it works:

1. Choose a landing sector. Six sectors, each based on a real Mars region (Gale Crater, Arcadia Planitia, Meridiani Planum, Elysium Planitia, Tharsis, Hellas Planitia), each with different sunlight, ice, radiation and building room.

2. Build and run a base for a crew of four over 30 sols (Mars days). Every building makes or uses power, oxygen, water or food, so every choice is a trade-off: cheap solar panels or a storm-proof nuclear reactor, radiation shielding or crop growth.

3. Survive Mars events: dust storms, solar particle events and equipment failures. Each event card offers real choices and ends with the true story it is based on (e.g. the 2018 dust storm that ended NASA's Opportunity rover).

4. Learn from failure: the mission can genuinely fail, and a debrief explains why in plain language, with the real science behind it.

Science: life-support numbers come from NASA's Life Support Baseline Values document, radiation from Curiosity's RAD measurements and NASA-STD-3001. All sources are listed in SOURCES.md in our repository.

Built with: Phaser 3, Vite and JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages. All game data (sectors, buildings, events, numbers) sits in editable data files, with automated tests.

Team: Amaleshwaren (code, testing), Pravin (testing), Avinesh (research, Presentation), Yogeswaran (art and design), Prasanna (art), Naavien (Research).

Next steps: playtests with 10 to 15 year olds, a classroom mode, and more real mission stories.
